lesson.title: From Coos to Sentences: The Sound Path Into Language
lesson.summary: Babbling and early speech trace a fairly predictable sequence, from early cooing through babbling to first words and simple word combinations, reflecting both maturing vocal control and growing linguistic knowledge.
lesson.body:
Before infants ever say a recognizable word, they move through a fairly predictable sequence of vocal development that lays the groundwork for spoken language. In the first couple of months, infants produce cooing sounds, mostly vowel-like noises. Around four to six months, this develops into babbling, repeated consonant-vowel syllables like ba-ba-ba or da-da-da, which reflects growing control over the vocal tract as much as it reflects any linguistic knowledge yet. This is one of the concrete, observable milestones that fits within the broader arc of language acquisition described earlier: an orderly, largely universal sequence unfolding on a roughly predictable timetable, shaped by both biological maturation and the language environment around the infant.

A striking and well-established finding is that babbling is universal across hearing infants regardless of what language or languages surround them, and that even deaf infants exposed to sign language will babble with their hands on a similar developmental timetable, producing repetitive, rhythmic hand movements that parallel vocal babbling. This is strong evidence that early babbling reflects a general biological readiness for language rather than simply imitating specific adult sounds. Over the second half of the first year, babbling gradually starts to narrow and take on the sound patterns specific to the language or languages the infant is actually hearing, a process sometimes described as babbling drift, so that by around ten to twelve months, a trained listener can often start to hear differences between the babbling of infants raised in different language environments.

The first recognizable words typically appear around twelve months, though there is real individual variation in exact timing. Early vocabulary grows slowly at first, often just a handful of words used to label familiar people and objects, and then accelerates, sometimes producing what researchers call a vocabulary spurt somewhere in the second year as children build up enough words and enough understanding of how naming works to add new words more rapidly. Around eighteen to twenty-four months, most children begin combining two words into simple phrases, sometimes called telegraphic speech because, like an old telegram, it strips out the small grammatical words and keeps mainly the essential content words, phrases like more juice or daddy go. From there, grammar becomes progressively more complex, sentence length grows, and children start applying grammatical rules productively, including the kind of predictable errors, like over-regularizing irregular verbs, that show a child is actively extracting rules rather than simply repeating memorized phrases. As with all developmental milestones, this sequence describes a typical range and order rather than a strict timetable every child must match exactly.
